latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Asymptomatic mucosal carriage of N. meningitidis in the nasopharynx. Necessary precondition for invasive disease; carriage 10-20% in healthy adults, peaks in adolescents 16-23y.
Penetration of mucosal barrier and entry of N. meningitidis into the bloodstream; window of typically <24h before fulminant disease.

Quantitative bloodstream pathogen load. In fulminant meningococcemia, blood bacterial loads reach 10^7-10^8 DNA copies/mL — among the highest in human bacteremia and tightly correlated with mortality.
Massive shedding of LOS-laden outer membrane vesicles drives plasma endotoxin levels orders of magnitude above other gram-negative sepsis. Plasma LPS strongly predicts shock and death.
TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10 surge driven by LPS-TLR4 signaling. Plasma TNF and IL-6 levels track severity and shock.
Massive complement activation through alternative and classical pathways with C3/C5 consumption. Anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) amplify shock.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Diffuse endothelial injury and glycocalyx shedding
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Direct adhesion of meningococci to endothelium plus cytokine/LPS-mediated injury → glycocalyx shedding, gap formation, exposure of tissue factor and subendothelial matrix.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Capillary leak with intravascular volume depletion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endothelial barrier failure causes massive third-spacing, hypovolemia, hemoconcentration despite total-body fluid overload; drives early shock.
Tissue-factor-driven thrombin generation with simultaneous consumption coagulopathy and impaired fibrinolysis (PAI-1↑). Acquired protein C and antithrombin deficiency typical and prognostic.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Acquired protein C / thrombomodulin pathway failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endothelial thrombomodulin and EPCR are downregulated, plasma protein C is consumed and degraded, producing severe acquired protein C deficiency that drives purpura fulminans.

Dermal microvascular thrombi with hemorrhagic skin infarction, classically progressing from petechiae to coalescing purpura to full-thickness necrosis within hours. Pathognomonic of severe meningococcemia.
Cytokine- and NO-mediated vasoplegia plus capillary leak plus septic cardiomyopathy → refractory hypotension; mixed distributive/hypovolemic/cardiogenic physiology.
Cytokine- and direct toxin-mediated reversible myocardial depression with reduced LVEF and elevated troponin; contributes to shock especially in children.
Bilateral adrenal cortical necrosis and hemorrhage from microvascular thrombosis; produces acute adrenal insufficiency and is found in up to 60% of fatal cases.
Functional consequence of WFS plus relative adrenal insufficiency of critical illness; contributes to refractory vasoplegia.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Peripheral limb / digit ischemia and gangrene
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Combination of microvascular thrombosis (DIC, purpura fulminans), low-flow shock and high-dose vasopressors produces peripheral and digital gangrene; major morbidity, often requiring amputation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Septic and ischemic acute kidney injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hypoperfusion, microthrombosis, cytokine-mediated tubular injury; also bilateral renal cortical necrosis in severe cases.
Pulmonary capillary leak, neutrophilic alveolitis, and cardiogenic component from septic cardiomyopathy → hypoxemic respiratory failure.

Hematogenous BBB crossing producing concurrent meningococcal meningitis. Present in roughly half of invasive meningococcal disease; outcomes diverge between meningitis-predominant and shock-predominant phenotypes.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: CSF bacterial proliferation and meningeal inflammation (subset)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: When BBB is breached: rapid CSF bacterial growth, neutrophilic CSF infiltration, and meningeal inflammation produce classic meningitis features overlaid on systemic disease.

Indolent intermittent fever, migratory arthralgia, and recurrent maculopapular/petechial rash over weeks without fulminant shock. Often associated with terminal complement deficiency. Rare but distinctive.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: requires mucosal breach, often after viral URI; impaired mucosal IgA
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Carriage is a near-universal precondition for invasive disease; only a small fraction of carriers progress.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: amplified when terminal complement (C5-C9) is deficient or eculizumab is in use
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Without intact MAC-mediated bacteriolysis, meningococci replicate exponentially in blood.
N. meningitidis sheds LOS-rich outer-membrane vesicles in proportion to organism load; plasma LPS scales with bacteremia.
LPS-TLR4 ligation triggers NF-κB and inflammasome activation with TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6 release.
LPS and bacterial cell wall activate alternative and classical complement; consumption produces hypocomplementemia.
TNF/IL-1 plus direct meningococcal-endothelial adhesion induce glycocalyx shedding, junctional disruption and tissue factor expression.
Loss of barrier function lets albumin and water shift into interstitium, producing intravascular hypovolemia despite tissue edema.
Endothelial tissue factor exposure and PAI-1 release drive thrombin generation and fibrinolytic shutdown.
Cytokine-mediated downregulation of endothelial thrombomodulin and EPCR plus protein C consumption produces severe acquired protein C deficiency.
Microthrombi in dermal vessels combined with hemorrhage from consumptive coagulopathy produce hemorrhagic skin infarction.
Acquired protein C deficiency is the dominant driver of purpura fulminans; severity tracks with protein C activity.
iNOS-derived NO and cytokine-mediated vasoplegia produce profound vasodilation and pressor-resistant hypotension.
Hypovolemic component layered on vasoplegia accounts for the early intense fluid requirement.
TNF/IL-1 directly depress myocardial contractility; LV dysfunction is prominent in pediatric meningococcemia.
Septic cardiomyopathy adds a cardiogenic component to mixed shock physiology.
Adrenal microvascular thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction follow systemic DIC; bilateral adrenal hemorrhage is the anatomical substrate of WFS.
Bilateral adrenal cortical destruction abolishes cortisol output; superimposed on relative adrenal insufficiency of critical illness.
Cortisol deficiency potentiates vasoplegia and pressor resistance; replacement reverses some pressor refractoriness.
Microthrombosis in distal arterioles produces digital and limb gangrene.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: amplified by high-dose vasopressors causing peripheral vasoconstriction
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Low-flow plus iatrogenic vasoconstriction worsens distal perfusion; classic pattern in pediatric meningococcemia survivors requiring amputation.
Hypoperfusion plus microthrombosis plus cytokine-mediated tubular injury produce septic AKI.
Pulmonary capillary leak with neutrophilic alveolitis produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema; resuscitation fluid loading exacerbates.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: occurs in roughly half of invasive meningococcal disease
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sustained high-grade bacteremia enables choroid plexus and cerebral microvascular crossing.
Once seeded, CSF lacks effective humoral and complement defense; rapid proliferation produces classic meningitis CSF profile.
Higher organism load yields earlier and more reliably positive blood cultures, though prior antibiotics dramatically reduce yield.
Quantitative PCR and culture density track bacteremia burden; very high loads are characteristic of meningococcemia.
Endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) raise the hypothalamic setpoint.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute-phase response.
Procalcitonin rises sharply in bacterial sepsis with endotoxin exposure; very high values typical of meningococcemia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: leukopenia (low WBC) is paradoxically a marker of severity in fulminant disease
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Most patients have leukocytosis with left shift; leukopenia signals overwhelming infection and worse prognosis.
Vasoplegia plus hypovolemia plus cardiac depression drives MAP below resuscitation thresholds.
Same mechanism as MAP; in children, hypotension is a late sign and prolonged capillary refill / tachycardia precede it.
Compensatory tachycardia precedes hypotension; commonest early vital sign abnormality.
Anaerobic metabolism from tissue hypoperfusion; lactate clearance is a key resuscitation endpoint.
Platelet consumption in microthrombi; thrombocytopenia is one of the most consistent labs.
Consumption coagulopathy depletes fibrinogen despite acute-phase rise.
Cross-linked fibrin degradation product; markedly elevated in DIC.
Factor consumption prolongs PT/INR.
Intrinsic factor consumption prolongs aPTT.
Direct readout of skin microvascular thrombosis with hemorrhagic infarction.
Petechial and purpuric eruption is the earliest visible sign and often pathognomonic; non-blanching.
Demarcation of digital and limb gangrene appears over 1-5 days; major driver of long-term morbidity.
Meningococcal purpura fulminans and necrotizing cellulitis can present with severe limb or soft-tissue pain before full demarcation of ischemia or necrosis.
Septic AKI raises creatinine; lags injury by 24-48h.
Oliguria precedes creatinine rise and is a key resuscitation endpoint.
Diffuse alveolar damage and pulmonary edema lower P/F ratio defining ARDS severity.
Shunt physiology lowers SpO2 despite supplemental O2.
Septic cardiomyopathy and demand ischemia produce troponin elevation correlated with mortality.
Hyponatremia from glucocorticoid+mineralocorticoid deficiency, often co-occurring with hyperkalemia.
Mineralocorticoid deficiency and AKI both raise potassium.
Cortisol deficiency can produce hypoglycemia, especially in children.
Bilateral adrenal enlargement with hemorrhage on CT/MRI is the imaging signature of WFS.
Neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis (typically 1000-10000 cells/μL).
Bacterial glucose consumption and impaired transport lower CSF glucose.
Inflammation increases BBB permeability raising CSF protein.
Meningeal inflammation produces neck stiffness; absent in meningococcemia without meningitis.
Hazard reads out the distributive-shock latent state directly.
Direct hazard correspondence.
Untreated adrenal insufficiency precipitates crisis with refractory shock and hypoglycemia.
Demarcated gangrene drives amputation in roughly 5-15% of survivors.
Direct hazard correspondence.
Direct hazard correspondence.
Consumptive coagulopathy combined with thrombocytopenia produces clinically significant hemorrhage.
Refractory shock is the dominant proximate cause of death; case fatality 20-50% in shock-predominant disease.
Severity of purpura fulminans is one of the strongest individual mortality predictors (e.g., GMSPS, Rotterdam scores).
Unrecognized WFS with adrenal crisis is a classic catastrophic terminal event.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: only when meningitis component is present and intracranial hypertension develops
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: When concurrent meningitis is severe, raised ICP can produce herniation; less common in pure meningococcemia.

Marked tachycardia precedes hypotension; rates 120-160 in adults, even higher in children.
Initially preserved by compensation, then abrupt collapse to <90 mmHg with vasopressor dependence.
Falls below 65 mmHg in shock; resuscitation target ≥65.
Tachypnea from acidosis and ARDS, 24-40/min.
Falls with ARDS; severe cases <90% on supplemental O2.
Oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/hr precedes creatinine rise.
Lowered by shock-related encephalopathy and (when present) meningitis; <12 in severe cases.
Bimodal: leukocytosis 15-30 typical; leukopenia (<4) is an ominous severity marker.
Marked neutrophilia with left shift; severe disease may show neutropenia.
Marked left shift, bands often >0.10.
Falls rapidly in DIC; severe thrombocytopenia (<50) common in fulminant disease.

Very high (often >10 ng/mL, sometimes >100) reflecting massive endotoxin exposure.

Rises with AKI and prerenal physiology.

Hyponatremia common, from SIADH (with meningitis) or adrenal insufficiency.
Hyperkalemia from AKI, mineralocorticoid deficiency, and tissue ischemia.
Hypoglycemia in children and in adrenal insufficiency; hyperglycemia from stress in others.
Falls with metabolic (lactic) acidosis.
Elevated in septic cardiomyopathy and demand ischemia; correlates with mortality.
Falls with ARDS; <300 mild, <200 moderate, <100 severe.
Composite organ dysfunction score; rises rapidly, scores >10 portend high mortality.
Subjective febrile prodrome present in nearly all cases, often abrupt onset.
Shaking chills frequent in early presentation.
Severe leg / back myalgia is a classic early symptom and red flag in adolescents.
Severe headache common, especially with concurrent meningitis.
Frequent early symptom, especially in children.
Non-blanching petechiae appear within hours, progress to coalescing purpura. Distribution: trunk, extremities, conjunctivae, palms/soles.
Coalescing purpura with full-thickness hemorrhagic skin necrosis; surface area extent strongly predicts mortality.
Severe soft-tissue or limb pain out of proportion to early visible findings, reflecting ischemic, necrotizing, or microvascular tissue injury.
Cool, mottled, demarcated digits / extremities progressing to dry gangrene over 2-7 days.
Prolonged capillary refill (>3s) and cold extremities are sensitive early signs of shock, especially in children.
Mucosal, GI, and venipuncture site bleeding from DIC.
Present only with concurrent meningitis subset; absent in pure meningococcemia.
Positive only with meningitis component.
Positive only with meningitis component.
Altered mentation from shock-related encephalopathy and/or meningitis.
Occurs mainly with meningitis component or hypoglycemia/hyponatremia.
Migratory arthralgia/arthritis in chronic meningococcemia and as immune-complex sequela in convalescence.
High in untreated disease (~50-90%); falls dramatically after even one antibiotic dose.
Among the highest in human bacteremia, often 10^4-10^8 DNA copies/mL; correlates with mortality.
Whole-blood meningococcal PCR retains positivity for hours-days after antibiotics; current gold standard for confirmation when cultures are negative.
Punch biopsy / aspiration of petechial lesion can show gram-negative diplococci even after antibiotics.
Elevated only with meningitis component; typically 1000-10000 with neutrophil predominance.
Neutrophil-predominant when meningitis present.
Elevated to 100-500 mg/dL with meningitis.
Markedly low (<40) when meningitis present.
Ratio <0.4 supports bacterial meningitis.
Elevated in bacterial meningitis (>3.5 mmol/L).
Gram-negative diplococci visible in 30-90% with meningitis component, sensitivity falls after antibiotics.
Sensitivity ~70-90% in untreated, much lower after antibiotics.
PCR retains sensitivity for days after antibiotics, very high specificity.
Elevated with meningitis (>20 cmH2O); high pressure predicts herniation risk.
Identifies Neisseria meningitidis as causal pathogen; influences age-specific epidemiology and chemoprophylaxis.
Distinguishes serogroups A, B, C, W, Y; B and C predominate in industrialized countries; W and A drive belt-region outbreaks. Determines vaccination strategy and outbreak response.
Phenotype dimension: shock-predominant fulminant, mixed sepsis-meningitis, meningitis-predominant, or chronic meningococcemia. Drives prognosis and treatment emphasis.
Binary indicator of meningitis component; ~50% of invasive meningococcal disease has meningitis. Activates meningitis-specific axes (CSF, neurologic).
CT/MRI bilateral adrenal enlargement and hemorrhage; the imaging signature of Waterhouse-Friderichsen.
Present with meningitis component on contrast MRI.
Diffuse swelling on CT/MRI when ICP is raised.
Bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest imaging when ARDS develops.
Inherited C5-C9 (or properdin) deficiency or functional deficiency from eculizumab/ravulizumab; massively elevates risk of meningococcal disease and recurrence.
Current or recent eculizumab/ravulizumab use induces functional terminal complement deficiency; up to 1000-2000-fold increased risk of meningococcal disease.
Anatomic or functional asplenia increases risk of severe disease from encapsulated organisms including N. meningitidis.
0=none, 1=incomplete, 2=complete MenACWY, 3=complete MenACWY + MenB. Reduces serogroup-specific risk.
Receipt of post-exposure rifampin/ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone reduces risk in contacts of an index case.
Near-universal susceptibility (>99%); reduced-susceptibility isolates rare but emerging.
Most isolates susceptible; intermediate and (rarely) penicillin-resistant strains exist regionally.
Whether the chosen antibiotic achieves CSF concentrations adequate to sterilize CSF (relevant when meningitis present).
Whether current empiric or definitive regimen actively covers N. meningitidis at adequate dosing.

Whether dexamethasone is given before or with first antibiotic dose; benefit established for pneumococcal meningitis, less clear for meningococcal but standard empiric practice in suspected bacterial meningitis.
0=none, 1=low-dose single, 2=moderate single, 3=high-dose single, 4=two pressors, 5=three+ pressors / refractory.
0=room air, 1=nasal cannula, 2=mask, 3=high-flow, 4=NIV, 5=invasive ventilation.
Hours from first symptom to antibiotic; outcome scales steeply with time-to-effective-therapy in meningococcemia.
Bimodal incidence: infants/young children and adolescents 16-23y; outcomes worse at extremes of age.
High in untreated disease and in pressor-dependent presentations.
Hazard of overt DIC; high in fulminant disease.
Refractory hypotension responsive to glucocorticoid replacement; classical Waterhouse-Friderichsen pattern.
Late-phase hazard once gangrene is demarcated; ~5-15% of survivors of severe disease.
Septic AKI hazard; KDIGO ≥1 in >50% of severe cases.
Hazard of P/F<300 with bilateral infiltrates not explained by cardiac failure alone.
Septic cardiomyopathy with troponin elevation, especially in pediatric meningococcemia.
Significant bleeding from DIC; intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleed, line-site oozing.
Hazard of intubation from ARDS, shock, or coma.
Risk in severe DIC, especially with thrombocytopenia and severely prolonged INR.
Active only with meningitis subset and raised ICP.
Long-term sequela of meningitis component; lower with N. meningitidis than S. pneumoniae but still material.
Hospital-acquired infection during ICU course; ventilator-associated pneumonia, line infections.
Overall case fatality 8-15%; shock-predominant fulminant form 20-50%, meningitis-predominant ~5%. Hazard concentrated in first 24-72h.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both consumed simultaneously in DIC; coupled drift beyond what mechanism edges already capture.
DIC severity raises D-dimer and consumes platelets in parallel.
Skin purpura fulminans precedes and predicts demarcated peripheral gangrene.
Higher lactate accompanies lower MAP through shared shock physiology beyond direct mechanism edges.
High-dose vasoconstrictors compound microvascular ischemia; iatrogenic contribution to peripheral gangrene.
Petechiae coalesce into purpura which then becomes fulminant; classic temporal progression.
CSF axes are activated only when meningitis subset is present; classification gates the meningitis CSF profile.
Each hour delay in effective antibiotic and resuscitation increases mortality; time-to-treatment is one of the few modifiable mortality factors.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Near-universal susceptibility; rare reduced-susceptibility isolates need penicillin MIC and alternative regimen.
Meningitic dosing (2 g IV q12h adult) achieves bactericidal CSF concentrations; subtherapeutic dosing fails.
Severe IgE-mediated reaction to penicillins precludes cephalosporin use; substitute meropenem or chloramphenicol.
Earliest possible administration (within hours) is the single most impactful intervention on survival.

failure_modes: subtherapeutic CSF penetration if non-meningitic dosing used and meningitis present
inadequate volume / pressor support undermining tissue antibiotic delivery

side_effects.interpretation: biliary sludge / pseudolithiasis especially in infants

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line empiric and definitive antibiotic for suspected or confirmed meningococcal disease at meningitic dosing.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cross-class susceptibility with ceftriaxone.
Adequate CSF penetration at meningitic dosing (2 g IV q4-6h).

treatments.context_specific_role: Equivalent alternative to ceftriaxone, used preferentially in neonates given ceftriaxone bilirubin displacement risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Most isolates remain susceptible but reduced susceptibility is regionally common; verify MIC.
Severe IgE-mediated reaction precludes use.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive narrow-spectrum step-down once N. meningitidis with confirmed penicillin susceptibility is identified; not used as initial empiric therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adequate CSF penetration at meningitic dosing.

failure_modes: seizure threshold lowering at high doses

side_effects.interpretation: rare seizure precipitation, especially with renal impairment

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative for patients with severe beta-lactam allergy where cephalosporins are not options.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Massive capillary leak demands large initial volume; balanced crystalloids preferred over saline.
Excess fluid worsens pulmonary edema; transition to vasopressors when MAP unresponsive to volume.

failure_modes: over-resuscitation worsening ARDS and tissue edema
treatments.context_specific_role: Initial resuscitation for distributive/hypovolemic shock; 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus typical first-line.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: First-line vasopressor for sepsis-induced vasoplegia; targets MAP ≥65.

failure_modes: exacerbation of peripheral ischemia at high doses
treatments.context_specific_role: First-line vasopressor for distributive shock not responsive to fluid resuscitation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Replacement-dose hydrocortisone is life-saving in Waterhouse-Friderichsen-related adrenal crisis.
Stress-dose hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) reduces vasopressor requirement in pressor-dependent septic shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stress-dose for vasopressor-dependent shock and Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal insufficiency.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric adjunctive dexamethasone is given for suspected bacterial meningitis before/with first antibiotic dose; mortality benefit best established for pneumococcal meningitis. Once meningococcal etiology confirmed, ongoing dexamethasone benefit is uncertain and is often discontinued.
Benefit requires dexamethasone before or simultaneous with first antibiotic; later dosing has no benefit.

failure_modes: no clear benefit in pure meningococcemia without meningitis
treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric for suspected bacterial meningitis pre-pathogen identification; benefit in confirmed meningococcal disease less robust than for pneumococcal.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Replacement is reserved for active bleeding or invasive procedures with severe coagulopathy; not given prophylactically by lab values alone.
Cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen <100-150 mg/dL with bleeding.

treatments.context_specific_role: Targeted replacement for DIC with bleeding or before invasive procedures; does not treat underlying DIC mechanism.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or uremia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Continuous RRT preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients with severe AKI complications.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Lung-protective ventilation (low TV, plateau <30) for ARDS; intubation also indicated for shock-related encephalopathy and airway protection.

failure_modes: ventilator-induced lung injury at non-protective settings
treatments.context_specific_role: Required for ARDS, refractory shock, or coma.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Eradicates carriage in close contacts within 24h; rifampin 600 mg q12h x 4 doses, single-dose ciprofloxacin 500 mg, or single-dose ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.

treatments.context_specific_role: Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts of an index case (household, daycare, intimate, healthcare with mucosal exposure); not a treatment of disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Patients with terminal complement deficiency or on eculizumab require both MenACWY and MenB plus often chronic prophylactic antibiotics.

failure_modes: serogroup mismatch (no protection against B if only ACWY given, or vice versa)
treatments.context_specific_role: Primary prevention; recommended for adolescents, asplenic patients, complement-deficient patients, eculizumab/ravulizumab recipients, microbiologists, travelers to meningitis belt, military recruits.

deficient.trajectory_modulation: Recurrent and atypical meningococcal disease; often non-groupable serogroups; recurrence common over years.

current_use.trajectory_modulation: Functional terminal complement deficiency; meningococcal disease with non-vaccine serogroups described despite vaccination.

asplenic.trajectory_modulation: Increased risk of fulminant disease from encapsulated organisms including N. meningitidis; OPSI-pattern presentation.

infant_under_1y.trajectory_modulation: Highest age-specific incidence; nonspecific presentation, rapid deterioration; serogroup B predominant in many regions.

adolescent_16_to_23y.trajectory_modulation: Second incidence peak driven by carriage; classic crowded-living context.

elderly_over_65y.trajectory_modulation: Higher case fatality despite lower incidence.

military_barracks_or_college_dormitory_o.trajectory_modulation: Outbreak risk via increased carriage transmission; hajj pilgrim outbreaks classically W135.

travel_recent.trajectory_modulation: Sub-Saharan African meningitis belt and outbreak regions during dry season; serogroup A historically, now W and C with vaccination changes.

smoking_present.trajectory_modulation: Increases nasopharyngeal carriage and acquisition; particularly in household contacts.

recent_uri.trajectory_modulation: Mucosal disruption facilitates invasion; classic prodrome before invasive disease.

immunocompromised.trajectory_modulation: Increased risk and severity; HIV particularly with low CD4.

fully_vaccinated_acwy_and_b.trajectory_modulation: Serogroup-specific protection; breakthrough disease usually with non-vaccine serogroups.

supportive_care: Immediate empiric IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) at meningitic dosing as soon as meningococcal disease is suspected — do not delay for lumbar puncture or imaging.
Aggressive volume resuscitation with balanced crystalloid (initial 30 mL/kg), with frequent reassessment for ARDS to avoid over-resuscitation.
Early vasopressor support with norepinephrine if MAP <65 despite fluids; add vasopressin or epinephrine for refractory shock.
Stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/day continuous infusion for vasopressor-dependent shock and suspected Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal insufficiency.
Targeted blood product replacement for active bleeding or before invasive procedures: platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate guided by labs and bleeding.
Lung-protective mechanical ventilation (TV 4-6 mL/kg PBW, plateau <30 cmH2O) for ARDS; consider prone positioning for severe ARDS.
Continuous renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or severe AKI.
Aggressive limb monitoring with pulse, perfusion, and compartment pressure assessment; surgical consultation for impending compartment syndrome or demarcated gangrene.
Adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h before/with first antibiotic dose for suspected bacterial meningitis (continue 4 days if pneumococcal; meningococcal benefit less robust).
Strict respiratory droplet precautions for first 24h of effective antibiotics.
Mandatory public health notification and identification of close contacts within 7 days before onset.

Post-exposure chemoprophylaxis for close contacts: rifampin 600 mg PO q12h x 4 doses, ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose; given within 24h of exposure identification when possible.
Audiology testing within 4-6 weeks of recovery for survivors with meningitis component.

Vaccination of household contacts when serogroup is vaccine-preventable; vaccination of the index patient on recovery as natural immunity is incomplete and recurrence is possible especially with complement deficiency.
Workup for terminal complement deficiency (CH50, AH50) in patients with recurrent meningococcal disease, infection with unusual serogroups, or family history.
Long-term wound care and rehabilitation for purpura fulminans / amputation survivors; psychological support for survivors and families given high acute mortality and lasting morbidity.
